worker_notes: Identity assessment: supplied candidate is a full article-body Europe PMC XML text parse, not merely an abstract or preregistration. Rand in Psychological Science; the supplemental-material DOI link identifies 10.1177/0956797620939054. Body includes both studies, methods, results and discussion. No source PDF supplied. Only es_value_o is assigned. Other side/fields are placeholders and must not overwrite existing verified fields. The main Study 2 veracity-by-treatment interaction directly tests the nudge effect on discernment. Preserve printed β = 0.039 without conversion or unsupported standardized-beta classification: Study 2 Analysis specifies rescaling sharing intentions from 1–6 to 0–1, not z scoring. Same-test p is printed p < .0001 (bound l), retained here only as contextual evidence because p is unassigned. Distinct printed tests are within-control discernment d = 0.050 and within-treatment discernment d = 0.142, and a post hoc item-level accuracy/treatment-impact correlation r(28) = .76; these do not estimate the main between-condition change in discernment. No statistic for a standalone nudge effect on false-headline sharing is substituted. No N derived.

coding_context.description: Giving people an 'accuracy nudge' before showing them headlines make them more discerning about their accuracy and less likely to share false articles on social media
coding_context.reported_success_quote: The first stage of the replication test ( n = 701) was unsuccessful ( p = .67). After collecting a second round of data (additional n = 882, pooled N = 1,583), we found a small but significant interaction between treatment condition and truth discernment (uncorrected p = .017; treatment: d = 0.14, control: d = 0.10). As in the target study, perceived headline accuracy correlated with treatment impact, so that treatment-group participants were less willing to share headlines that were perceived as less accurate.
